claim: Dryden's 2004 paper proves only a partial (finite-ambiguity) generalization of Huber's theorem to hyperbolic orbisurfaces: the Laplace spectrum determines cone-point orders only up to finitely many possibilities, not exactly.
stance_target: the manuscript's priority claim of being first to give exact finite-coefficient determinacy
quoted_support: Theorem 4.5. If two compact orientable Riemann orbisurfaces are Laplace isospectral, then we can determine their length spectra and the orders of their cone points, up to finitely many possibilities.

claim: Dryden 2004 proves isospectral sets of compact orientable hyperbolic orbisurfaces of genus >= 1 have finite cardinality, generalizing McKean's finiteness theorem for Riemann surfaces.
stance_target: existing finiteness results for hyperbolic-orbisurface isospectral sets
scope_conditions: compact orientable hyperbolic orbisurface of genus g >= 1
quoted_support: Theorem 5.1. Let O be a compact orientable Riemann orbisurface of genus g ≥ 1. In the class of compact orientable hyperbolic orbifolds, there are only finitely many members which are isospectral to O.

claim: The finiteness proof uses the Selberg trace formula and diameter/trace bounds on Dirichlet-polygon generators, not heat-trace coefficient counting, so it is not a finite-coefficient determinacy result in the manuscript's sense.
stance_target: the manuscript's priority claim is not anticipated by Dryden 2004, which uses a fundamentally different (non-heat-coefficient) mechanism
quoted_support: Theorem 4.5 tells us that the Laplace spectrum determines (up to finitely many possibilities) the length ℓ(Q) of a shortest closed path... By choosing our generating set to be the set of side-pairing elements of a Dirichlet polygon P for Γ, we can easily bound the traces of hyperbolic conjugacy classes.

claim: Dryden's math/0411290 was never independently journal-published; its results were folded into her 2004 Dartmouth PhD dissertation and effectively superseded on the exact-determinacy side by the later Dryden-Strohmaier paper.
